summary: A mixed number (2¾) and an improper fraction (11/4) name the same quantity in two forms. Converting between them rests on 'how many wholes fit', because b copies of 1/b rebuild one whole (b/b = 1). So 11/4 = 8/4 + 3/4 = 2 wholes and 3/4 = 2¾; reversing, 3⅖ = 3 wholes = 15 fifths, plus 2 fifths = 17/5. Ground the work in iterating unit fractions past the whole (counting quarters past 4/4) rather than a bare rule, and treat improper fractions as legitimate numbers.
misconceptions: Mixed→improper adds the whole to the numerator: 3⅖ → (3+2)/5 = 5/5
Multiplies but forgets to add the numerator (15/5), or concatenates the digits (32/5)
Believes an improper fraction is 'not allowed' and must always be written as a mixed number

activities.title: Stamp quarters past the whole and watch wholes form
steps: On a number line marked in quarters, add one quarter at a time, counting aloud: 1/4, 2/4, 3/4, 4/4.
At the 4th quarter, group the four quarters into one whole unit; do the same again at the 8th quarter.
Keep going to the 11th quarter and read off what you have: two whole units with three quarters sitting past them, so 11/4 = 2¾.
Now work the other way for 3⅖: break each of the 3 wholes into fifths (one whole = 5 fifths, so 3 wholes = 15 fifths), then add the 2 extra fifths to get 17/5.
Keep the denominator unchanged throughout, and say the running total in both forms as you go.
activities.insight: The improper form and the mixed form mark the SAME point: every b copies of 1/b fuse into one whole, and each whole breaks back into b pieces. This is why you multiply 3 × 5 (each whole is 5 fifths) and then add the 2, not add the whole to the numerator.

activities.title: Convert both directions and verify by reversing
steps: Convert 11/4 to a mixed number and 3⅖ to an improper fraction, showing your working for each.
For the improper→mixed task, state how many wholes you found and how many pieces are left over.
For the mixed→improper task, say out loud what the first product counts (e.g. '15 counts the fifths in 3 wholes') before adding the leftover pieces.
Check each answer by converting it back to the other form and confirming you return to where you started.
Also write 6/5 + 4/5 = 10/5 as both an improper fraction and a whole number (2).
activities.insight: Fluent two-way conversion with a reverse-check confirms the forms are equal and that improper fractions such as 7/4 or 17/5 are valid answers, not mistakes to be 'fixed'.

activities.title: Reveal the wholes hidden inside an improper fraction (support)
steps: Look at a bar showing 11/4 drawn as individual quarters.
Circle or mark off the complete groups of four quarters, naming each group as one whole.
Read what is left after grouping and write the mixed number: 2 wholes + 3 quarters = 2¾.
activities.insight: An improper fraction already contains whole groups; finding them is a matter of grouping b pieces at a time, with the leftover pieces naming the fraction part.

checkQuestion: Say: 'Convert 11/4 into a mixed number, and convert 3⅖ into an improper fraction. Show me how you work each one out.' Watch the method for each — do not tell them a rule.
checkAnswer: 11/4 = 2¾ (8/4 = 2 wholes, 3/4 left over); 3⅖ = 17/5 (3 wholes = 15 fifths, plus 2 fifths = 17/5), denominator unchanged.
